w: What's tested hCG: where it comes from, how it saves the corpus luteum, and that a pregnancy test measures it Milk: prolactin makes it, oxytocin lets it down, progesterone holds it back until delivery, dopamine keeps prolactin low, and prolactin stops periods How a sperm gets into the egg: ZP3, ZP2, and the block on a second sperm; and capacitation first Where the pregnancy hormones come from: estriol needs the baby's help, progesterone doesn't Implantation, the placenta's other hormones (hPL and relaxin), and what starts labor Dr. Madison's lecture follows a pregnancy from start to finish, with the focus on hormones: getting sperm and egg together, implantation, the placenta and its hormones, labor, breastfeeding and birth control. These notes follow his recording and slides. A quick review of the cycle After ovulation, the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum. It makes progesterone, the key hormone that gets the uterine lining ready for an embryo: wider vessels and stored sugar (glycogen). If there's no pregnancy, the corpus luteum dies after about 14 days, becomes a scar called the corpus albicans, the hormones crash, and the lining is shed. Getting sperm to the egg About 250 million sperm go in, and only about 50 reach the far end of the fallopian tube, where the egg is usually fertilized. Sperm can fertilize for 24 to 48 hours. At ovulation estrogen is in charge, and it helps the sperm three ways: it buffers the vaginal pH (makes it less acidic), it thins the cervical mucus, and it makes the uterine muscle (the myometrium) contract to push sperm upward. The egg's three layers From the outside in: the cumulus cells (he called them the corona radiata), the zona pellucida (a thick capsule), and the egg's own membrane. The sperm's acrosome, a cap full of enzymes, digests its way through. Fertilization The sperm first binds ZP3 on the zona, and that sets off the acrosomal reaction: the acrosome bursts and releases its enzymes. ZP3 is cleaved away, and the sperm binds ZP2 next. Then the egg finishes its second meiotic division (the first was at ovulation), and the cortical reaction sheds the rest of the zona proteins so no other sperm can get in. One sperm, one egg. The two pronuclei fuse, and you have a zygote. Memory trick: ZP3 comes first, as in "3, 2, go." Capacitation Fresh sperm can't fertilize yet. In the male tract, cholesterol keeps their membrane stiff so the acrosome can't burst early. In the female tract they lose that cholesterol, calcium can get in, blocking proteins are removed, and the tail switches from a wave to a whip. Now the acrosomal reaction can happen. The fallopian tubes The finger-like fimbriae catch the egg. Cilia and muscle contractions move it along. Fertilization usually happens in the far (distal) part of the tube. Estrogen holds back, progesterone lets in Right after ovulation estrogen is still high, and it squeezes the opening into the uterus, holding the embryo back while the lining gets ready. When progesterone rises, the muscle relaxes and the embryo moves in. Remember: estrogen contracts, progesterone relaxes. The first week Fertilization happens within a day of ovulation. The embryo reaches the uterus about 4 days after ovulation and implants 5 to 7 days after. About 8 days after ovulation it starts making hCG. The blastocyst The embryo implants as a blastocyst: a ball of cells with a fluid-filled space. Its outer layer is the trophoblasts, the cells that do the implanting. He said you don't need the names of the earlier stages. Implantation The blastocyst puts out sticky adhesion molecules, enzymes (proteases) and hormones (hCG). The lining gets ready too, which is called decidualization: more blood vessels, more glycogen, and a calmer local immune system so the embryo isn't attacked as foreign. When it sticks, the trophoblasts split into two kinds. Cytotrophoblasts are the nurse cells. Syncytiotrophoblasts are the invaders: they push enzymes into the lining to dig in, and they make hormones (hCG and hPL). With progesterone's help, the lining cells swell with glycogen and become decidual cells that feed the embryo until the placenta is ready. hCG saves the corpus luteum hCG comes from the trophoblasts. It tells the corpus luteum "we're pregnant," so it doesn't die. The corpus luteum keeps making progesterone and estrogen, even more than before. LH and FSH stay low, so there are no more cycles and no periods. A pregnancy test measures hCG. It shows up in urine or blood about 10 to 11 days after fertilization and peaks around 10 weeks. Side notes from his slides: hCG can weakly turn on the thyroid's TSH receptor, causing a short-lived overactive thyroid. Estrogen raises the thyroid's carrier protein, so total thyroid hormone goes up but free hormone barely changes. Corpus luteum, then placenta The corpus luteum makes most of the progesterone and estrogen for the first trimester. The placenta starts growing after implantation, is finished by the end of the first trimester, and takes over. The placenta It trades gases and food, makes hormones, protects the baby from many infections while letting the mother's antibodies through, and sends the baby's waste back to the mother. Oxygen, water and nutrients go to the baby; carbon dioxide and waste come back. Some drugs and viruses get through too. hPL Human placental lactogen, also called human chorionic somatomammotropin, helps the breasts develop. It also works against insulin: it breaks down fat, sugar and protein to keep fuel flowing to the baby. So pregnancy is insulin resistant, with high insulin levels, and some mothers get gestational diabetes. It has many causes, genes included. Relaxin Made by the corpus luteum (because of hCG) and the placenta. It keeps the uterus quiet so the baby doesn't come early, loosens the pelvic ligaments and softens the cervix. Making the pregnancy hormones It all starts with the mother's cholesterol. The placenta makes progesterone by itself. Estrogen needs teamwork. The main estrogen of pregnancy is estriol (estradiol is the normal cycle's, estrone is menopause's). The placenta is missing one enzyme, 17,20 desmolase, so it hands the job to the baby. The baby's adrenal gland makes DHEA sulfate, the baby's liver changes it, and the placenta's aromatase turns it into estriol. That's why the mother's estriol shows how healthy the baby is. Labor Labor comes about 40 weeks after the last period started. The baby stretches the uterus. The uterus makes more receptors for oxytocin and the prostaglandin PGF2 alpha. The balance tips toward estrogen, so the muscle contracts. Prostaglandins raise calcium in the muscle for stronger contractions, and PGE2 softens the cervix. Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary is the big one: it drives contractions, and more contractions bring more oxytocin. After birth, oxytocin keeps the uterus contracting, which stops heavy bleeding. Getting the breast ready During pregnancy, estrogen grows the ducts and adds fat, progesterone adds alveoli (the milk-making sacs), and prolactin and cortisol build up the milk-making enzymes. But progesterone blocks prolactin, so full milk waits for delivery. After delivery Progesterone drops when the placenta comes out, and prolactin is free to make milk. Oxytocin squeezes the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli, and the milk comes out (letdown). Prolactin makes it, oxytocin lets it down. Controlling prolactin and oxytocin Normally the brain keeps prolactin low with dopamine. Suckling lowers dopamine, so prolactin rises. Suckling also releases oxytocin from the posterior pituitary. High prolactin blocks GnRH, so LH and FSH fall and periods stop. That's why breastfeeding mothers often have no periods. He said to focus on dopamine. Birth control Three ways. Stop ovulation: the pill, whose estrogen blocks the LH surge (it also thins the lining and thickens mucus). Keep sperm and egg apart: barriers and others he skipped. Stop implantation: high-dose estrogen (a lining that grows but never gets progesterone's preparation), the IUD, or drugs that block progesterone's receptor. Progestin makes the cervical mucus thick so sperm can't get in.
